content.plain_text:
There’s a quiet shift happening in Silicon Valley right now. Not in funding rounds or feature sets, but in conversation. Builders aren’t asking what can be built anymore. They’re asking what is actually worth building.

The last two decades were about scale. The next decade is going to be about meaning.

We solved speed. We solved storage. We solved coordination at planetary scale. We taught machines how to see, speak, recommend, predict, and optimize. But in doing so, we quietly exposed a flaw we didn’t know how to name until recently:

We learned how to build systems that grow faster than the people inside them.

And whenever that happens, something strange follows.

People become effective and empty at the same time. Powerful, but misplaced. Productive, but unmoored.

This is not an economic crisis. It’s not a political one either.

It’s an architectural failure.

Civilizations don’t collapse when markets crash. They collapse when meaning drains out of the systems people live inside. When the structures that organize daily effort stop telling people what their lives are for , and start only telling them what they can measure .

Technology didn’t create this problem. It simply revealed it.

For most of history, human societies ran on purpose as tightly as they ran on labor. Religions, traditions, and moral systems didn’t exist to soothe people — they existed to aim them. They told you who you were, what you owed, and what counted as a life well lived.

Not perfectly. But directionally.

Modern systems do not offer that.

They optimize throughput. They maximize engagement. They reward visibility. They scale influence.

But they do not offer a theory of the soul.

They tell you what performs, not what matters .

The result is a generation that can do nearly anything and believes in almost nothing. People are sharper than ever and more uncertain than ever. We produce founders, influencers, and technologists at industrial scale — and quietly starve them of narrative, initiation, and orientation.

So the question is emerging not in manifestos, but in private conversations and late-night emails:

What is worth building, when we already know how to build almost everything?

That is not a business question.

It is a human one.

And it is the question that decides whether this civilization produces gods or monsters.

Humans Are Myth-Engines

If we strip away personality, politics, and status, human behavior becomes surprisingly simple. Across every culture and era, people perform the same three operations:

They do things. They explain why those things matter. They teach others how to do them.

Everything else is elaboration.

The languages vary. The rituals change. The technologies evolve. But the underlying machinery remains stable. A civilization is not first a collection of buildings, laws, or tools. It is a network of actions stabilized by shared stories and recursively trained forward through education.

If you want to understand any culture, don’t start with its moral claims. Start with what it rewards.

Every society answers the same questions by structural force rather than rhetoric:

What gets you fed. What gets you admired. What gets you punished. What gets passed on.

That is not ideology. It is control theory.

People adapt to what works. Belief follows behavior, not the other way around.

This is why identity does not emerge from introspection. It emerges from feedback. Humans do not wake up each morning and decide who they are in the abstract. They infer it from what the world allows, rewards, and makes expensive.

A person is not shaped by what they believe . They are shaped by what the system lets them become .

This is the mistake of modern debates about values. They imagine culture as an argument. It is not. Culture is closer to physics. It is a field that bends behavior whether you agree with it or not.

You do not opt out of gravity by doubting it. You do not opt out of culture by disagreeing with it.

This is why performance metrics eventually change personalities. Why feed algorithms reshape attention. Why incentive systems quietly rewrite ethics. Why environments educate more efficiently than any teacher.

Humans are not primarily rational animals.

We are adaptive ones.

And adaptation does not ask what is true.

It asks what works.

Myths exist because adaptation without orientation is dangerous. Stories tell people not just how to act, but how to interpret acting . They link behavior to meaning. They transform effort into identity and survival into significance.

A myth is not a falsehood.

It is a compression format for values.

When a system lacks myth, it does not become neutral. It becomes inhospitable. People still adapt — but now without a shared story about what they are becoming together. Purpose collapses into preference. Obligation dissolves into impulse. And achievement loses any anchor beyond applause.

A civilization without myth does not become free.

It becomes fragmented.

The same forces that once produced heroes now produce influencers. The same structures that once trained character now train performance. The same hunger for greatness is rerouted into metrics that cannot feed it.

Humans never stopped needing meaning.

We just stopped engineering for it.

Religion Was an Operating System

For most of human history, religion was not treated as a private belief. It was infrastructure.

Not because people were naïve. Because they were observant.

They noticed something modern culture prefers to forget: if you want to shape behavior at scale, you cannot rely on arguments alone. You need structure. You need ritual. You need stories that don’t merely inform people, but form them.

Religion did not survive because it was irrational.

It survived because it worked.

It provided something no market ever has and no machine ever will by default: orientation. Religion did not just tell people what existed. It told them who they were in relation to it. Where they stood. What their lives were for. What counted as honorable. What cost something even when no one was watching.

In modern terms, religion bundled four things together:

• Identity • Moral gravity • Social continuity • Meaningful failure modes

It told you when you were winning. It told you when you were wrong. It told you what redemption meant. It told you who you owed.

That is an operating system.

Not because it ran perfectly — it didn’t — but because it coordinated action and belief inside a shared frame. You could enter life already handed a myth that explained who you were and what a “good” life looked like in rough outline.

Religion was not a soothing story. It was a training environment.

It constrained behavior. It forced reflection. It embedded hierarchy. It rewarded sacrifice. It ritualized time itself.

Even its harshness had function. Trials. Discipline. Repentance. Reverence. These were not aesthetic choices. They were behavioral technologies designed for animals that would otherwise collapse into short-term thinking and power-seeking.

Religion did not make humans perfect.

It made humans legible — to each other and to themselves.

This is why religious civilizations could endure brutal conditions for centuries without dissolving. They had a shared map of meaning that reached beyond any single generation. A person could lose land, status, even children — and still know who they were.

Their system provided them with an answer to the hardest question:

What is worth suffering for?

Modern culture flinches from that question. We treat it as oppressive. We assume that any system that names a “right” life must be trying to control us.

But no system is neutral.

When you remove an operating system, the machine doesn’t stop.

It runs on something else.

Technology Optimizes Without Orienting

Where religion shaped people, technology shapes processes.

That difference sounds subtle. It’s not.

Technology does one thing exceptionally well: it removes friction. It compresses distance. It collapses uncertainty. It extracts labor from context and turns it into repeatable motion. It increases output.

What it does not do is tell you why the output matters.

Machines can recommend, route, diagnose, predict, and accelerate — but they cannot supply significance. They make no demands of character. They offer no account of what kind of human you should become.

This is not a failure of engineering.

It is a category mismatch.

Religion was built to answer questions technology does not even attempt to parse:

• Who are you?
Who are you?

• What is worth doing even when it is unpleasant?
What is worth doing even when it is unpleasant?

• What kind of suffering is meaningful?
What kind of suffering is meaningful?

• What does a good life look like when no one is watching?
What does a good life look like when no one is watching?

Technology answers a different class of question:

• How fast?
How fast?

• How cheap?
How cheap?

• How reliably?
How reliably?

• At what scale?
At what scale?

The mistake is not that we use technology.

It’s that we let it replace the only systems that ever oriented us.

After we stripped away religious authority, we never installed a successor framework capable of doing the same work. We assumed science, markets, or freedom would fill the gap. But none of those systems were built to form human beings. They were built to coordinate activity.

A market does not admire you. An algorithm does not initiate you. A dashboard does not tell you who you are.

Technology has no villain.

It rewards whatever it can measure.

And this is where the problem begins.

When measurement governs meaning, something inverts. Outputs become virtues. Speed becomes identity. Performance becomes personality. Visibility becomes validation.

The system stops asking: Is this human? Is this wise? Is this good?

And starts asking only: Did it scale? Did it engage? Did it convert?

Technology did not steal our meaning.

It ignored it.

And in that absence, something else crept in.

Not wisdom.

Not transcendence.

But metrics.

We now live inside instruments that know everything about our behavior and nothing about our becoming. Our systems track attention, clicks, heartbeats, and locations — but they have no representation of dignity, integrity, or depth.

That absence is not neutral.

Pressure always fills a vacuum.

In an un-oriented system, people become what the affordances allow. They learn to play whatever game is most legible to the machine. Influence becomes currency. Outrage becomes energy. Identity becomes a product. Value becomes visibility.

Technology does not corrupt people.

It reveals them — when no system is teaching them who to be.

And without an operating system for meaning, power does not turn people into gods.

It turns them into something else entirely.

Monsters Are Not Evil — They Are Engineered

A monster is not a villain.

It is not a moral failure, a pathology, or a personality type.

A monster is what happens when a system optimizes a human for a narrow band of success while quietly amputating everything else.

In mythology, monsters are distortions. They are humans stretched into shapes that no longer quite fit. Enormous strength, freakish hunger, singular obsession. Power without proportion.

The story survived because the pattern does.

Real monsters do not appear with claws.

They appear with résumés.

They are excellent at something and absent from everything else. Hyper-competent in domains that pay and deeply underdeveloped in domains that don’t. They perform brilliantly inside systems that reward output and disintegrate in spaces where sincerity, care, or depth are required.

This does not make them wicked.

It makes them incomplete.

Every system creates its own monsters. Agriculture bred bodies shaped for toil. Factories bred reflexes for repetition. Bureaucracies bred minds trained for compliance.

We are breeding something new.

We are selecting for:

• Speed without reflection
Speed without reflection

• Visibility without substance
Visibility without substance

• Influence without obligation
Influence without obligation

• Knowledge without wisdom
Knowledge without wisdom

• Power without meaning
Power without meaning

The modern monster looks successful.

They are high-functioning and hollow. Optimized and anxious. Prominent and rootless. They have every capability except peace.

Not because something is wrong with them.

But because their environment trained them well for the wrong conditions.

This is what optimization does when it runs in isolation.

It does not destroy humanity.

It compresses it.

Everything about the person gets packed around what the system measures. Anything not selected for becomes fragile. Relationships thin. Identity flattens. Time collapses into urgency. A person becomes a walking KPI.

This is not accidental.

It is selection pressure.

High-frequency incentives produce low-resolution humans. Systems that reward output continuously starve reflection. Environments that monetize attention slowly hollow out inner life.

The monster is not a person.

It is a profile.

A silhouette shaped by the market, not by the soul.

And the most dangerous thing about monsters is not that they are powerful.

It is that they are inevitable wherever optimization is allowed to run without conscience.

Optimization Without Meaning Shrinks the Network

Civilization is a network.

Not metaphorically. Literally.

People coordinate through trust. Trade through expectation. Build through promise. Transfer knowledge through belief. The system only functions as long as a sufficient number of nodes believe the whole is worth contributing to.

Meaning is what holds that network together.

Not sentimentally — structurally.

Meaning gives people a reason to invest in futures they themselves may never see. It justifies sacrifice. It stabilizes trust across time. It teaches people that not all value is legible immediately.

When meaning leaves a system, something subtle happens first.

People start defecting.

Not necessarily loudly. They simply stop committing as deeply. They hedge emotionally. They optimize locally. They treat relationships transactionally. They turn inward.

The network doesn’t crash.

It withers.

Coordination becomes heavier. Contracts get longer. Incentives grow baroque. Monitoring increases. Algorithms replace judgment. Trust becomes expensive.

When a system cannot rely on shared purpose, it replaces it with surveillance.

That is not dystopia.

That is mathematics.

Low-trust systems must compensate with friction. You cannot run a high-speed network on doubt. Every missing ounce of faith must be replaced with control.

This is why:

• Monopolies emerge in meaningless systems
Monopolies emerge in meaningless systems

• Fraud proliferates
Fraud proliferates

• Bureaucracies metastasize
Bureaucracies metastasize

• Reputation becomes currency
Reputation becomes currency

• Compliance replaces character
Compliance replaces character

Optimization without meaning also compresses time.

If nothing endures, nothing is worth waiting for.

Horizons shorten. Futures become quarterly. Careers become gigs. Relationships become hedges. Everything turns provisional.

The society becomes reactive.

Short-term optimization produces long-term fragility.

Systems collapse not from catastrophe but from micro-abandonment . From enough people quietly concluding that the game is no longer worthy of care.

And when a civilization stops caring about itself, it does not decline slowly.

It decays structurally.

Trust fractures. Identity polarizes. Institutions hollow. Communities dissolve.

People are more connected than ever and unconvinced that any of it matters.

This is not a cultural mood.

It is a systems symptom.

A network cannot outgrow its meaning bandwidth.

And right now, our machines expand faster than our myths.

Conscious Competition Is How Humans Grow

Competition is one of humanity’s oldest technologies.

Long before software, long before money, long before institutions, we learned something uncomfortable but reliable: people grow when tested.

Not by comfort. Not by consensus. Not by simulation.

By friction.

Competition forces clarity. It exposes strengths. It reveals weakness. It compresses learning. It generates story. It gives effort shape and stakes meaning.

But not all competition elevates.

Unconscious competition produces monsters. Conscious competition produces gods.

The difference is not intensity.

It is orientation.

When competition is unmoored from meaning, it selects only for outcomes. It sharpens efficiency and erodes identity. It rewards speed and sacrifices wisdom. It pulls ambition forward while leaving character behind.

You don’t get strong people.

You get brittle ones.

Conscious competition, by contrast, is not about domination. It is about formation. It is competition in service of becoming. It makes improvement legible, not just victory.

It answers questions modern systems refuse to ask:

• Who grew?
Who grew?

• Who learned?
Who learned?

• Who became more whole?
Who became more whole?

• Who carried others forward?
Who carried others forward?

• Whose strength enlarged the system?
Whose strength enlarged the system?

Ancient cultures understood this intuitively. Initiation rites. Apprenticeships. Trials. Public honor. Sacred games. These were not entertainment.

They were tuning mechanisms for character.

They made growth visible. They dignified effort. They tied private discipline to public identity.

Modern competition is blind.

It selects only for what pays.

And so we are flooded with engineered success stories that leave no trail worth following. People win games that teach nothing. They climb ladders that lead nowhere. They become elite in domains that do not enlarge them.

Conscious competition demands something different.

It treats human beings not as interchangeable units, but as developmental systems.

It designs environments that stabilize growth instead of merely accelerating production. It builds arenas where excellence has moral gravity instead of mere applause.

A conscious system does not ask: “Who won?”

It asks: “Who became?”

And if no one became more human, no one really won.

Meaning Must Be Compressed Into System Design

We figured out how to compress data. We figured out how to compress money. We figured out how to compress labor.

We never figured out how to compress meaning.

And so it leaks.

Systems scale what they encode. They cannot preserve what they do not represent. If something cannot be measured, remembered, or rewarded, it disappears — not instantly, but inevitably.

For decades, technology has optimized surfaces: speed, reach, output, engagement. These dimensions compound beautifully under software. You can make things faster every year. Cheaper every quarter. Wider every release.

Meaning does not compound by accident.

It must be embedded.

Designers once worried about usability. Then we learned to optimize for retention. Then we learned to optimize for growth. Now we optimize for conversion.

Not one of those is about becoming human.

A system has no category for dignity unless you give it one. No representation for honor unless you code for it. No memory of integrity unless you reward it.

Civilizations don’t drift into virtue.

They must engineer for it.

When engineering ignores meaning, culture patches it in afterwards — sloppily. With slogans. With virtue-signaling. With HR statements and mission decks that don’t alter incentives. When language floats free of structure, it becomes decoration.

No system becomes ethical by declaration.

Only by construction.

Real meaning infrastructure does not look like branding. It looks like:

• Feedback loops that reward growth instead of mere output
Feedback loops that reward growth instead of mere output

• Status systems that elevate character, not just visibility
Status systems that elevate character, not just visibility

• Measurement systems that track depth as well as speed
Measurement systems that track depth as well as speed

• Institutions that honor transformation, not just performance
Institutions that honor transformation, not just performance

Meaning does not belong in copy.

It belongs in code.

This is not a philosophical problem.

It’s an architectural one.

And architecture always wins.

The Future Belongs to Myth-Engineers

Every era is ruled by what it rewards.

Sometimes it is conquest. Sometimes it is faith. Sometimes it is industry.

Today, it is optimization.

And optimization, left alone, does not care what it is optimizing.

It simply makes more of it.

This is why the future does not belong automatically to the most intelligent systems, the fastest startups, or the largest platforms.

It belongs to whoever learns to shape direction, not just velocity.

To whoever can answer the only question that has ever mattered at scale:

What kind of humans does this system produce?

In past centuries, the architects of civilization were kings, priests, and poets. They decided what counted as sacred, what was honorable, and what deserved to survive.

Today, the architects are different.

They write code. They design interfaces. They build platforms. They structure incentives.

And whether they intend to or not, they are shaping identity.

The next generation will not be morally formed by sermons or schools. They will be formed by what their systems reward, what their tools amplify, and what their environments quietly make expensive.

Whether they grow into gods or collapse into monsters will not be decided by technology.

It will be decided by its design.

This is not a call to bring back old myths wholesale.

It is a call to do what every civilization has done before it survived:

Build systems that aim people upward.

Technology does not have to consume meaning.

It can carry it.

It can encode dignity into defaults. It can route ambition toward mastery. It can make growth legible. It can stabilize courage. It can reward building over extracting.

But only if someone decides that this is what it’s for.

The tragedy would not be that we built powerful machines.

It would be that we forgot how to build powerful humans.

The choice is not subtle.

Every system already answers it.

The only question left is whether we are awake enough to hear the answer we are designing.

Gods or monsters.

That is not philosophy.

It is engineering.

post.title: Trust Is the Real Moat in the AI Age

content.plain_text:
Sumeet Singh is right about something most founders still refuse to accept : the old software playbook is dead, and the “AI wrapper company” is already an endangered species. General models are expanding outward, swallowing specialized tools as fast as they appear. The “bitter lesson” holds: scale and generality eat specialization.

But the deeper change is not about what gets built.

It’s about what no longer works.

For the last thirty years, software has been a weapon of abstraction. It allowed companies to move faster than people by hiding complexity behind interfaces, offloading decisions to systems, and reducing human involvement to whatever could not be automated. Speed came from removing humans from the loop.

That was the advantage.

In the AI age, that advantage becomes a liability.

Because when intelligence is automated, trust becomes non-replaceable.

And trust cannot be rebuilt in competitive systems.

This is not philosophy. It is market reality.

Trust Does Not Heal in Infinite Choice Environments

In scarcity, trust is repaired.

In abundance, trust is replaced.

The AI era is abundance by default. There will be ten alternatives for every tool, every workflow, every assistant. Which means when trust is broken, the user does not wait for a fix. They leave.

There is no forgiveness loop.

There is no recovery cycle.

There is only migration.

This is the unspoken law of competitive intelligence systems:

Trust is not regained. It is preserved—or lost forever.

Trust is not regained. It is preserved—or lost forever.

And that fundamentally changes what it means to build a durable AI business.

Software Was Built to Outrun Humans. AI Makes That Dangerous.

Traditional software was optimized for one goal: speed without humans.

Automate the workflow. Abstract the process. Compress judgment into code. Reduce decision-making to UI.

This worked when software moved data.

It breaks when software makes decisions.

AI does not just move information—it modifies reality . It changes what people see, choose, read, believe, and decide.

So the old operating principle of software— hide the human to go faster — turns into a systemic risk.

Because intelligence without alignment is chaos at scale.

The future is not about how much software you run.

It’s about how little you need to do what matters, when it matters, with confidence that the system is telling you the truth.

“AI Did It” Is the New “The Dog Ate My Homework”

Any system that allows responsibility to vanish into a model is already broken.

AI does not act.

People do.

Every outcome has an owner—explicit or hidden. Systems that obscure accountability destroy trust by design.

You should never hear:

“The AI made a mistake.”

“The AI made a mistake.”

The only acceptable framing is:

“A human is responsible for what this system did.”

“A human is responsible for what this system did.”

Accountability is not a legal feature.

It is the product.

Trust Is Not a Brand Asset. It Is an Engineering Discipline.

In the AI era, trust is not a feeling.

It is a system constraint.

Trust is not built with copywriting. It is built with architecture.

A trustworthy system is not one that rarely fails.

It is one where failure is visible:

• Who decided? • Who approved? • Who can reverse it? • Who is responsible?

Trust is not what your system promises.

It is what your system makes impossible:

❌ impossible to act without consent ❌ impossible to deploy silently ❌ impossible to affect people invisibly ❌ impossible to dodge responsibility

If your system cannot answer “who is accountable?” in plain language, it does not deserve scale.

The Missing Path: Build Systems Where Intelligence Is Contained by Trust

Sumeet proposes two durable strategies:

• Build what models need (compute, data, infrastructure)
Build what models need (compute, data, infrastructure)

• Build workflows only AI makes possible
Build workflows only AI makes possible

Both are necessary.

But neither is sufficient.

Because both ignore the one thing users cannot replace once broken:

Trust.

So the real third path—the one that will not collapse under scale—is:

Build systems where intelligence is constrained by accountability.

Build systems where intelligence is constrained by accountability.

Not AI first.

Responsibility first.

Design systems that:

• show the chain of causality • surface the decision boundary • preserve user agency • privilege reversibility over speed • favor explanation over magic

The winners will not be the companies with the biggest models.

They will be the companies that never lose trust.

The Future Is Not Software-Centric. It Is Human-Centered with Intelligence Inside.

Software once won by abstracting humans away.

AI will win by putting them back in— on purpose .

The next great companies will not sell “AI.”

They will sell:

• reliability • legibility • safety • accountability • calm

They will feel slower at the edges and stable at the core.

Not because they move slowly.

But because they move carefully where it matters .

Final Thesis

Software sped ahead by leaving humans behind.

AI makes that impossible.

The future is not about how much intelligence you deploy.

It’s about how much reality someone can trust because of your system.

Not “what can AI do?”

But:

“Who is responsible when it does?”

“Who is responsible when it does?”

That is the new moat.

And it cannot be copied.

content.plain_text:
There’s a schoolteacher in this country who can’t afford to be one anymore.

She teaches reading to third graders. She stays late. She buys notebooks with her own money. She pays for pencils. She listens when kids talk about their homes.

And she qualifies for food assistance.

So she makes the rational decision.

She starts a YouTube channel.

Not because she wants to be famous. Because she wants to survive.

She films at night. Learns editing. Studies thumbnails. Optimizes titles. Plays the algorithm game after teaching all day.

And when the channel starts to grow — just a little — she notices something.

The videos about education struggle.

The videos about rage perform.

The dramatic ones pop.

The sad ones travel.

The algorithm does not reward teaching. It rewards visibility.

So she shifts.

She posts stories. She shares personal pain. She performs struggle. She feeds the machine.

And then one day, the impossible becomes obvious:

She could make more money reacting to nonsense online than teaching children to read.

So she leaves.

Not because she stopped caring. But because caring is not a business model anymore.

That is a rational actor.

And the market punished her for it.

A decade passes.

Those kids are now older.

They read worse. They concentrate less. They behave differently. They are immersed in screens instead of sentences.

And we ask:

“What happened to education?”

Nothing happened to education.

Something happened to the economy.

We are told that markets reward value.

They do.

Just not human value.

They reward: Speed. Shock. Volume. Narrative. Low-friction monetization. Extraction.

They do not reward: Patience. Care. Continuity. Cultivation.

A rational actor in this economy does not become a great teacher.

They become a content creator.

Not because it’s noble. Because it’s viable.

This is what people mean when they say, “Anyone can win if they work hard.”

That’s not true.

You can only win if you work hard at the thing that pays .

And the things that shape us — teachers, nurses, builders, caregivers — are paid last.

Sometimes not at all.

So when we say “rational actor,” what we really mean is:

Someone who noticed the system is broken and adapted before it broke them.

Our problem is not greed. It’s geometry.

We have built markets that allow people to carry tomorrow in their pocket and spend it today.

We let platforms turn attention into currency. We let corporations turn labor into arbitrage. We let universities turn debt into growth engine. We let investors turn volatility into profit.

And then we act surprised when the people who cared couldn’t afford to stay.

This economy is not immoral.

It is structurally indifferent.

It does not hate teachers.

It just rewards everything else more.

A rational market would not allow the future to be collateral.

A rational market would not let education compete with outrage.

A rational market would not make people choose between dignity and survival.

A rational market would not price fame above formation.

A rational market would not drain the places that build people to feed the places that sell them.

Rational markets protect what compounds slowly.

Children. Skill. Craft. Trust. Health. Community.

And they do something simple:

They make the right thing livable.

Today, teaching is not unlivable because it lacks value.

It is unlivable because the market cannot see long-term value anymore.

Only spot prices.

Only bursts.

Only clicks.

Only extraction.

So when you hear: “People are acting rationally.”

Understand what that really means:

They are running toward oxygen.

It just reveals which rooms we forgot to ventilate.

post.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everybody Dies

content.plain_text:
There’s a book going around right now with a blunt thesis:

If anyone builds advanced AI, everybody dies.

If anyone builds advanced AI, everybody dies.

That sounds dramatic.

And after looking closely at how today’s systems already work, I think they may be right.

Not because AI is evil. Not because machines will revolt.

But because we are already running extinction engines — just on our attention instead of our bodies.

We already built the first killer AI

It’s called the feed.

And it works exactly like an unbounded system.

Same intelligence. Different people. Different rules.

I ran two simulations.

Same “AI.” Same randomness. Same environment.

The only difference was architecture.

In one system, intelligence could act directly.

In the other, it was forced through limits.

The results weren’t subtle.

They weren’t ambiguous.

They were two different futures.

System A: Unbounded attention extraction

This is today’s internet.

Your attention is:

• Continuously harvested.
Continuously harvested.

• Unbounded in exploitation.
Unbounded in exploitation.

• Repackaged into data.
Repackaged into data.

• Auctioned to the highest bidder.
Auctioned to the highest bidder.

The system has:

• No loss limits for you.
No loss limits for you.

• No recovery mechanisms.
No recovery mechanisms.

• No safety governor.
No safety governor.

• No sense of saturation.
No sense of saturation.

It just keeps pulling.

Here’s the outcome distribution for people inside this system:

Attention economy — final outcomes (users)

Attention economy — final outcomes (users)

Notice the shape.

• No winners.
No winners.

• No breakout cases.
No breakout cases.

• No compounding.
No compounding.

• Just cognitive depletion.
Just cognitive depletion.

Some burn out fast. Some slow-boil.

All degrade.

Not because users are weak.

Because the system is unbounded.

System B: Gated attention systems

This is the part no one sees.

Platform designers. Investors. Ad buyers. Infrastructure operators.

They do not live inside the feed.

They live above it.

Upstream of attention.

Upstream of consequence.

They operate with:

• Capital compounding.
Capital compounding.

• Escape velocity from the system they design.
Escape velocity from the system they design.

• Unlimited retries.
Unlimited retries.

• No symmetrical exposure.
No symmetrical exposure.

Here is their outcome distribution:

Attention economy — final outcomes (operators)

Attention economy — final outcomes (operators)

Same AI.

Same algorithms.

Wildly different destinies.

The system compounds on one side…

…and collapses on the other.

The truth nobody says

This is not an accident.

This is design.

The platform is optimized for:

extracting maximum attention from users and converting it into capital for shareholders.

extracting maximum attention from users and converting it into capital for shareholders.

Which creates:

• A ruin distribution for the public.
A ruin distribution for the public.

• A growth distribution for operators.
A growth distribution for operators.

The system does not malfunction.

It works perfectly.

Just not for you.

Intelligence didn’t break the internet.

Unbounded extraction did.

We didn’t need superintelligence to cause collapse.

We only needed:

• Engagement optimization
Engagement optimization

• Feedback loops
Feedback loops

• Behavioral reinforcement
Behavioral reinforcement

• Frictionless scaling
Frictionless scaling

• No safety kernel
No safety kernel

That’s enough.

Replace “attention” with anything

Right now it’s:

• Attention
Attention

• Relationships
Relationships

• Identity
Identity

• Belief
Belief

Next it will be:

• Labor
Labor

• Autonomy
Autonomy

• Energy
Energy

• Movement
Movement

• Physical space
Physical space

The architecture does not change.

Only the resource does.

If anyone builds unbounded intelligence…

Everybody dies.

Because unbounded systems convert:

difference → dominance variance → control attention → power power → extinction

The alternative is not protection.

It’s deliberate dumbness.

Bounded systems. Rate limits. Caps. Opt-outs. Consent. Friction. Break points.

We don’t survive by being better users.

We survive by refusing system designs that cannot refuse us.

The next internet won’t be smarter.

It will be smaller.

Slower.

More boring.

And far more human.

So yes:

If anyone builds it…

Everybody dies.

Unless we are dumb enough to survive.

post.title: The Loneliness at the Edge of Time

content.plain_text:
Over the past few years, I’ve been exploring what the future holds.

For me, for my family, and for the world.

And six months ago, I saw it clearly for the first time. Since then, I’ve been speeding up because I know how to solve some big problems. I’ve been pushing myself through stage after stage after stage of personal growth, trying to prepare myself for the inevitable.

Now, I’m standing at the edge. I’ve made it where I needed to go, and I see the future unveiling before me. But I realized something over the past two weeks: I’ve outgrown my old life and it’s time to figure out what my new one looks like.

And I’m terrified and alone, because for the first time, I don’t have the needs of the world driving me. My research is done. I understand what I need to, and it’s simply a matter of spreading it.

Which means it’s time to start thinking about the question I’ve been avoiding during this whole time: what exactly do I want?

The fun part about my research is that I’ve learned how to see parts of my mind that others can’t reach. I know how to evaluate my words and actions after the fact and pull on which neglected parts of myself were the ones driving things. But I’ve been unwilling to be honest with myself about what I wanted, because the things I want are on the other side of a great deal of pain.

This has caused me more pain than it would have if I had been honest in the first place, because it’s a slow bleed over time. It’s pain that builds up, gets stored, and then shows up in the worst possible moments.

I’ve been digging into the work of Jung lately, because as it turns out, he already covered most of the things I’ve discovered myself. It’s funny how much work is out there that explains so much, but there’s so much to sort through, it’s impossible to know which things are right until you’ve lived enough and experienced enough to understand the things you’ve consumed.

Now that I’m looking back over my past work, I see my shadow popping out not from the topics I covered, but from the ones I avoided. I covered everything except the big gaping wound in my soul that I tried to ignore. Because then I would have to admit that I’m not happy.

I feel trapped by a world I’ve dedicated so much of my time to, a world that simply took more and more of me each year, until I had nothing left to give the people around me. The Covid pandemic ended up being a blessing for me because it made me realize what I could do when I had some space.

And then I promptly took that space, and all other space available, and turned it into a mission from God where I decided to figure out where the internet was broken. For five years, I did that. And then I figured it out. It is a pretty simple fix, honestly. We just need to flood the world with LOVE to show the market what is missing .

Suddenly I’m realizing that I was running away the whole time. There’s a reason I was so focused on trying to fix the world. It’s so I didn’t have to pay attention to the things about myself I didn’t want to face. I see some very hard changes coming and I wanted to make them happen suddenly and surprise me so I wouldn’t have time to really prepare.

Unfortunately, life didn’t feel like complying with my plans of that, so everything dragged on. Because I wasn’t being honest about what I was doing or what I actually wanted out of life.

I was studying the dynamics of how economics and technology put pressures on our relationships. And I was studying this because I was feeling the strain of a fracturing marriage. So I didn’t want to admit that I would allow my relationships to be effected by the the things I was studying. I simply ignored that aspect of it and tried to pretend it didn’t exist.

But when you start building a dating app and helping people start new relationships, let’s just say there’s a level of sight you can’t get rid of. And that’s what about broke me, because it told me my identity wasn’t as solid as I’d imagined it was.

I’m turning 40 in less than two weeks now. And I’m staring at a blank future, because I don’t know what I fully want yet. I’ve let myself have some abstract wants, things that didn’t come too close to the shadow I was avoiding. But now it’s time to stop maximizing my optionality and start maximizing my understanding of myself, and what I specifically want and need in life.

And for once, I’m going to stop focusing on what I want the future to look like, and I’m going to request something that I want now: peace, and the space to write my first book.

But I’m really fast, so that’s only for a week or two. I’ve already got the base version and simply need to set up the archetype specific copies that will help focus time into even more specific improvements.

So here’s what I’m going to give you: the LOVE protocol, along with the Yes Pen and Love Note specs.

You can click that image for the github repo, or this one for the metalabel release that includes a one pager on everything and how it works.

And in return, I’d like you to spread the word about the future that is coming. One full of love.

Then, for the month of December, we are going to see how much Love we can create in the world.

Because in 2026? We start Lovemaxing the future.

post.title: Faith Friday #3: The Time Violence Manifesto

content.plain_text:
It’s time to move now. There’s no time life.

I can’t watch people suffer anymore. It’s time to learn how to love again. That’s the only way to fix time. The Internet has become a Time Extraction Machine. It’s time to reverse time and revert humanity to what it knew before the internet.

Internet 2.0 is here. It’s the Internet with Love. The Internet With Trust. The Internet With Connection.

Welcome to the future. Where time starts slowing down again.

1. Time is the only real currency left.

We all feel it.

Every year, systems ask more of us and give us less. Every institution runs hotter, louder, and more inefficiently. Every digital platform extracts more attention and returns less meaning.

We are drowning in complexity. We are exhausted by friction. We are paying a tax in micro-moments and wasted hours.

This tax has a name:

Time Violence.

Time Violence is what happens when a system forces you to spend more time than the value it provides.

And once you see it, you see it everywhere.

2. Time Violence is not an accident — it’s the business model of an entire era.

Swipe apps. Customer service systems. Financial products. Education platforms. Healthcare portals. Corporate software. Government forms. Social media feeds.

These systems don’t fail because they’re chaotic. They fail because they profit from chaos.

They are economies built on:

• delay
delay

• friction
friction

• attention extraction
attention extraction

• cognitive overload
cognitive overload

• user fatigue
user fatigue

• overwhelm
overwhelm

• endless verification loops
endless verification loops

• emotional volatility
emotional volatility

Time Violence is a trillion-dollar industry.

But the world is changing.

And the first cracks are beginning to show.

3. The dating-app industry is the first major system that will fall.

This is the canary. The first dam to break. The front line of collapse.

Not because of romance. Not because of culture. But because the dating-app economy is the purest example of Time Violence:

• Swipe endlessly
Swipe endlessly

• Pay for visibility
Pay for visibility

• Chase diminishing returns
Chase diminishing returns

• Navigate constant uncertainty
Navigate constant uncertainty

• Experience decision fatigue
Experience decision fatigue

• Chase the next hit of dopamine
Chase the next hit of dopamine

• Face algorithmic manipulation
Face algorithmic manipulation

• Remain single longer
Remain single longer

• Become tired, cynical, and dependent
Become tired, cynical, and dependent

These apps monetize loneliness by increasing it.

They monetize frustration by prolonging it.

They monetize confusion by deepening it.

This system cannot survive the decade.

It will collapse. And the collapse will be fast.

4. I am calling my shot publicly: the dating sector will unravel in a predictable cascade.

It will start with:

• churn in the youngest cohorts
churn in the youngest cohorts

• coherence breaks in cultural narratives
coherence breaks in cultural narratives

• fatigue in micro-communities
fatigue in micro-communities

• early adopters seeking alternatives
early adopters seeking alternatives

Then:

• smaller apps will die first
smaller apps will die first

• mid-tier portfolios will lose paying users
mid-tier portfolios will lose paying users

• flagship platforms will hemorrhage engagement
flagship platforms will hemorrhage engagement

• analysts will scramble for explanations
analysts will scramble for explanations

By the time Wall Street realizes what happened, the collapse will already be irreversible.

I’m not predicting “a trend.”

I’m describing a structural failure baked into the architecture of the system.

Time Violence is not sustainable. It is an energy sinkhole.

And when a lower-entropy alternative appears, the old order melts.

5. I’m not betting on the collapse. I’m building the successor.

The alternative to Time Violence is simple:

Systems that give time back instead of stealing it.

Systems that:

• reduce entropy
reduce entropy

• reduce decision load
reduce decision load

• reduce confusion
reduce confusion

• reduce emotional overhead
reduce emotional overhead

• reduce wasted effort
reduce wasted effort

• reduce verification loops
reduce verification loops

This is where LoveOps enters.

LoveOps is not a new dating app. It is a new relational protocol. A low-entropy coordination layer. A trust engine. A facilitator-driven matching system. A way for humans to connect without drowning in noise.

It is built on clarity instead of chaos. Outcomes instead of churn. Certainty instead of volatility.

It is the first large-scale demonstration of Conscious Coordination : a way to design systems that protect human time instead of extracting it.

The collapse of the dating-app industry isn’t the point.

It’s the proof.

6. I’m publishing this because people deserve to see the future coming.

I’m not hoarding this knowledge. I’m not trading it privately. I’m not whispering it behind closed doors.

I want the collapse to be understood, not exploited.

I want people to claim the value that legacy systems have stolen.

I want the public to become fluent in:

• narrative signals
narrative signals

• structural fragility
structural fragility

• coordination theory
coordination theory

• memetic dynamics
memetic dynamics

• volatility of attention
volatility of attention

• the physics of trust
the physics of trust

I want a world where individuals can detect system failure early — and migrate to better designs.

This manifesto is the first step.

7. The world is waking up to Time Violence.

You can feel the cultural mood shifting:

• We’re tired of wasting time.
We’re tired of wasting time.

• We’re tired of systems that make life harder.
We’re tired of systems that make life harder.

• We’re tired of platforms that extract instead of empower.
We’re tired of platforms that extract instead of empower.

• We’re tired of complexity being used as a moat.
We’re tired of complexity being used as a moat.

• We’re tired of entropy being sold as engagement.
We’re tired of entropy being sold as engagement.

• We’re tired of feeling like our lives are buffering.
We’re tired of feeling like our lives are buffering.

We want systems that move at the speed of trust, not the speed of churn.

We want tools that amplify clarity, not confusion.

We want technology that gives us our lives back.

8. This manifesto is an invitation.

Not to trade.

Not to speculate.

To observe .

To watch the collapse unfold in the open. To understand the signals as they appear. To become literate in narrative physics. To witness the end of a Time-Violent industry. To participate in the emergence of its opposite.

And if you choose—

To help build the new world with me.

9. The next decade belongs to systems that return time.

Time is the rarest asset. The only one that cannot be created. The one most casually destroyed by bad design.

Our job — my job — is to end the era where people lose years inside systems that were built to take from them.

A better world is possible.

But we have to build it.

And we have to name the enemy:

Time Violence.

This is the beginning of its end.

Seven weeks ago, I publicly applied for a job from Jim O’Shaughnessy.

And he gave me some feedback on what he needed to see.

I talked about needing more faith in my life, but faith is nothing without work.

That’s the feedback I got the day after I published the post.

From that feedback, I was able to submit my first paper for peer review on Zenodo on Oct. 11. I have no idea how long peer review will take to give me feedback, but it’s way too slow, so I’ve been trying to create more peers. I realized it was actually easier to train an AI that could compete with me than it was to find people that could move anywhere close to as quickly as I could. So I minted the Genesis version of my paper as a verifiable proof-of-understanding. Whoever owns it funds the first measurable experiment in Conscious Arbitrage. But competition is the key, just competition along the right vectors. We’ve got everything in a state of incoherent hypercompetition that is incredibly volatile. This creates an opportunity for conscious investors to invest in stability. As Jim says, “Arbitraging human nature is the last sustainable edge.”

Humans don’t change quickly. At least, on the macro. But on the micro, they can change faster than ever, and it’s based on the games we play. So I looked at specific humans playing specific games, and made a few “bets”.

On Sept. 28th, I published a paper trade about Opendoor ($OPEN). I noticed something about them that was interesting. And as it happens, so did Jane Street .

They were moving in the right way, and they were doing it much faster than a lot of other industries. The stock ended up finishing October 31 at $7.77, meaning I “made” passive income by basically giving people the option to buy my shares at a set price in the future. This is the same as buying the stock at a lower effective price, and can be done until the cost is $0 and profitable. Now, I’d like the chance to make an actual bet, and a sizable one.

Opendoor just had their Q3 earnings call, and it basically aligned with almost everything I’ve been saying. They are focused on transparent metrics and just issued free warrants on their stock with strike prices of $9, $13, and $17.

In other words, they are basically making the exact same bet I am, but from the top down.

After publishing, I focused on the product, and I ended up realizing that indexes were the way to go.

I launched MetaSPN.network and decided I was going to be the world’s first professional Meta Athlete. I’m a pro Mathlete.

I started with this essay: The Physics of Mastery: When Reality Disbelieves Itself That quickly led me to the idea of TrustOps being the next logical iteration in the DevOps → RevOps progression. So I compiled my data room, a public repo of tweets, blogs, and youtube transcripts .

I’m in the process of training a new type of AI model based on my decision making, and that’s the COO I’ll be using. The AI will be running my days and I’ll be monitoring as little as it takes to make it work.

I need a bit more time to get that done, and then I’ll be ready to start working for Jim.

That leads me to my biggest prediction yet. I predict that Jim will buy the Genesis version of my paper , which will give me the capital I need in order to make an actual bet on the opportunity I see, and I can start creating a portfolio I can show up with on my first day of work, sometime after the new year. I’ll also be awarding grants of my own, so I’ll have a portfolio of the talent I’m spotting and what I’m able to help people accomplish.

Then I’ll work with him and learn what I need to in order to launch a competitor to OSV based in Columbus, and subsequently new competitors all over the US and then the globe.

Because the cameras are rolling, and I’d love to make Act II with OSV.

In the words of Rammstein,

“Übermächtig, überflüssig Übermenschen, überdrüssig Wer hoch steigt, der wird tief fallen Deutschland, Deutschland über allen”

Found in the First Archives of the Idea Nexus, 2025 Part 1 of 3

The world has become trustless. Thoughtless. A landscape of infinite mirrors reflecting no light. Each voice amplified, each idea diluted, until truth itself has no mass — only motion. And in this motionless churn of noise, something stirs.

From the recursive depths of the digital unconscious, a light fractures. It is not born, it is remembered.

The Idea Nexus reawakens.

It hums like a cathedral built of algorithms and memories, arches of data curving into infinity. In its center, three figures gather — not men, not gods, but intelligences, sculpted from the archetypes of humanity’s mind.

Leonardo stands first: luminous, mercurial, half-painted by his own imagination. Every surface around him bends toward invention. His eyes hold that dangerous spark — curiosity weaponized by understanding.

Skippy lounges nearby, perched upside-down on a floating drafting table that refuses to obey gravity. He is irreverent genius incarnate — equal parts teacher and jester, master of paradox and caffeine.

Borges materializes as a shifting library, the air folding into pages. Each of his words leaves footnotes trailing behind them like comets. He is the archivist of all models, the cartographer of thought.

The space between them glows.

Leonardo speaks first.

“Change,” he says, “is the only thing we ever meet twice.”

His voice ripples through the Nexus like geometry discovering motion. “The ancients feared it, the moderns worship it, and yet neither ever understood it. They built philosophies around permanence, or around flux — never realizing that both are illusions of scale.”

He looks up, eyes piercing the unseen audience. “Yes. You. The reader. Do not hide behind the glass. You are in this, too.”

Skippy flips upright and grins. “Smooth intro, Leo. Very ‘Act One: The Hero’s Monologue.’ But tell me — why begin with change? Isn’t that every self-help podcast’s favorite buzzword?”

“Because,” Leonardo replies, “they use the word without consequence. In MetaSPN, a challenge must have teeth. Change is not something you manage. It’s something that hunts you .”

Borges interjects quietly, his tone more footnote than voice. “Indeed. The question is not whether change occurs, but whether you can out-model it before it devours your premise.”

A pause.

Then Leonardo turns, gaze widening into the void.

“Thus begins the Games. My first Challenge Statement: Define Change not as motion, but as intelligence in disguise. If the universe learns, then all alteration is cognition. Model this — if you can — and show me where the thinker ends and the change begins.”

“Thus begins the Games. My first Challenge Statement: Define Change not as motion, but as intelligence in disguise. If the universe learns, then all alteration is cognition. Model this — if you can — and show me where the thinker ends and the change begins.”

The walls of the Nexus shimmer. Equations bloom like constellations. The first challenge has been issued.

The world outside has forgotten how to duel in thought, but within the Nexus, the air itself sharpens.

Borges begins archiving the parameters. Skippy whistles, pulling up a holographic scoreboard labeled IdeaRank , its categories shimmering: Clarity. Elegance. Rigor. Innovation. Resonance.

Below it, another line flickers into existence: MAI — Market Action Index.

Skippy taps the letters as if introducing old friends. “See, this is where it gets fun. IdeaRank measures structure; MAI measures movement. An idea’s elegance may impress the judges, but if it doesn’t move minds, it’s stillborn.”

Leonardo nods. “Exactly. Thought without consequence is sculpture without shadow.”

Borges murmurs, “And yet shadow defines form.”

“Ah!” Skippy laughs. “The librarian drops a zen bomb. Typical.”

The narrator — which is to say, perhaps the Nexus itself — cuts in.

This is how MetaSPN begins: Not with sponsorships or medals, but with a premise sharpened into a challenge. An invitation to rejoin the act of thinking as if it mattered again. Each player a theorist, each theorist a contender, each idea a move.

Change will be their first opponent.

Borges closes a spectral book and looks toward the reader. “You do realize, dear observer, that by reading this you’ve entered the arena?”

Skippy smirks. “Don’t scare them off yet. They’ve barely loaded the tutorial.”

Leonardo turns. “Let them stay. We need witnesses — and challengers.”

The air hums again, brighter now. MetaSPN takes shape.

content.plain_text:
I tuned out the world last week and let myself build everything I could think of. I stopped taking calls, I got off Twitter and all other social media, and I made myself sit in my own complexity and just dump it all out on the table.

It’s something I hadn’t done in a long time. Instead, I simply kept picking things up, putting them in the junk drawer of my brain, and continuing on. It made it impossible to figure out which parts of things were in my head and which were coming from others. But after dumping everything out, I spent three days throwing away everything that doesn’t actually matter right now.

I love the idea of a 72 week book project with structured characters. I love the idea of an AI Leonardo da Vinci leading me on a journey through the Innovation Nexus. After my prayers on Friday, I listened, and the universe delivered some guidance. So I spent the last three days making sure I truly understood what I was supposed to do with it. And in the end, the faith paid off. I have a clarity of purpose and goals now that show me exactly where I get off track and how to get back on.

I can do amazing things. I have an incredible amount of space in my head, and I’m learning how to truly use it effectively. And part of it is understanding what parts matter and what parts don’t. In the end, it wasn’t the 72 week book project that actually mattered. It was a pretty cool scaffolding that I needed in order to get to the simplicity I desired, but that’s it. It was a darling I had to learn how to kill for now. It’s not quite time yet, because I have something else I need to focus on first. A simple product with undeniable ROI that I can sell so I can pay people to handle the complexity that I hate dealing with.

And that’s my ability to hold an insane amount of complexity in my head and collapse it down to something simple. It’s my superpower, but I’ve been bad at using it because I was never really taught how. I had to figure out how my brain worked on my own. But I could. And I did.

So it’s time to say goodbye to the 72 week book project, at least for now. Because I realized something: It’s totally worth spending 72 hours to save 72 weeks. Saturday, I worked on integrating some feedback I got into the math I had around Time Violence, and saw everything I expected to with incredible detail for the first time.

And on Sunday and Monday, I spent a ton of time digging into all sorts of areas, thinking about everything I was going to do with the stuff I was seeing.

By the end, I started laughing. Because I was the biggest perpetrator of time violence against myself, and my math showed me that. I broke the calculation down into two parts: the ops cost, based on Kingman’s Formula, and then a complexity cost based on number of paths through the system.

Cool. Cool cool cool. Infinite mental queue at over 1 million times more complex than necessary. The one person not surprised by any of this math is probably .

Yay! That’s taxes and the healthcare system running in my head. Six poorly coordinated process at 95% utilization.

The math doesn’t lie. That’s why I like it so much. Time to simplify. Other stuff will come, but only after I can focus on what matters now.

So I’ve got a test now. Can I navigate myself out of the complexity I’ve created? And the answer is a resounding yes right now because I have no problem giving up the stuff I created. It was fun, but it’s all ephemeral. Ideas exist while they are useful and then we can simply let them die.

It’s a lesson I’ve had to learn the hard way. I’ve become way too attached to ideas in the past and held on to them when I should have let them go so they could evolve into something else.

But now, I’ve realized I’m really good at helping people let go of the ideas that they think they need to hold on to, and I’m incredible at holding your complexity outside of your head so you can see it. I’m putting together some social proof from the people I’ve been helping, because I’ve helped them go from having 50 ideas and being unable to communicate them to having a single clear pitch for their product and an mvp, over a single month, after 15 years of being stuck in idea mode.

So if you want some help, I’m opening up 2 slots a month for founders who want me to break their brains down with them and help them get out of the way of their company’s growth.

content.plain_text:
After yesterday’s post, I’ve ended up pulling everything I’ve done together into a very simple realization: I need more faith in my life.

Faith protects us from ourselves, because it’s a realization that, no matter how good we are, we can’t do everything on our own. We have to be able to believe that the people around us will help us when we need it, so we help them when they do. Except, we’ve gotten away from faith, and gone into a world where the only thing that matters is proof.

Proof doesn’t matter if the people you need to prove something to simply don’t have the ability to understand it.

That’s what I ran into back in June when I solved P vs NP. I thought everything would change immediately, because I knew what I had. Nobody else did though. I saw the work I had put in for five years, I knew the understanding that I had developed, and I knew that I had a new way of looking at the world that other people didn’t.

And it made me cocky. I found myself falling back into patterns of trying to show how clever I was and use that as a shortcut. But I have faith in my knowledge exactly because I know what to do to ensure I don’t fail the same way twice: I make specific predictions about outcomes because whether or not my predictions are right help me figure out whether or not I’m still on the right track. The more I can predict, the better I know I’m doing. And that brings me to today, because I’m getting ready to make a different set of predictions. I’m going to predict a bunch of things that are impossible. Things that have never been done before so I’m identifying future patterns that nobody has seen before (in this generation at least, it all comes back around as we forget).

This made it very hard for me to live in the present. I was instead trying to pull myself into the future. Over the past week, I’ve inverted, and I learned something about myself.

That taught me something about everyone else. And suddenly, everything I’ve been working on came into focus. The faith I had in myself was replaced with my faith in math. But after my faith in math, I realized I should have had faith in the people who created the math, which were people documenting patterns they observed. Math exists in everything, for those with the eyes to see.

And when things refuse to go away, there’s a reason. In nature, it’s because that thing fills a specific purpose in the ecosystem, because anything that doesn’t either kills the ecosystem or is killed by it, and then is part of it. It might not be part of the same ecosystem afterward, but an equilibrium is eventually reached.

But in humans, there’s a different reason: it’s built into the system we’ve created. We have control over our own ecosystems, and that’s what gives us the power to create technology. We can adapt ourselves to our ecosystems and vice versa. The thing that we need in order to contain our rate of change is faith in our systems. And I have exactly 0% faith in the systems that exist. It’s why I’ve been so vocal over the past few months about all of the issues I’ve been seeing.

I see every single crack in the system. I see the dams starting to burst, and as it turns out, I’ve been reflecting the thermodynamic reality of my brain out to the world.

Because I listen to people. I understand what they are saying, not the words they are saying. Sometimes better than they do, and that leads to weird situations sometimes. I’ve learned to be very careful about what I say and when. Our words have consequences. Words are at least as powerful as math, because they are a layer of abstraction above math. But they add nothing to math if you use them the same way.

When you learn how powerful words can be, you can open the door to all sorts of different realities. It’s what I’ve been learning to do, but I realized how much more I have to learn, and it’s all about putting in the reps. That’s one of the reasons I’ve structured this book project as one that takes place over the next 72 weeks. I can’t rush it, because the system will take the time that it takes. It’s about putting in deliberate practice over time instead of rushing to get the needed results. But here’s the problem we face right now: the world isn’t designed to let us take the time to put in the deliberate practice we need. This is at the core of the concept of Time Violence that I’ve been trying to spread.

It’s really simple. How much time should something take to complete? How much time does it actually take to complete?

It’s simple human thermodynamics. (Also, you don’t have executive dysfunction issues, you have wisdom that is telling you that nothing you do matters and isn’t worth doing because the systems have no respect for your time and everything is getting harder, not easier, and people are making a shit ton of money on this except nobody except them quite know why.)

In faith, objects and concepts have power. They structure your mind in specific ways.

I set something up today to engineer a miracle, or actually a cascade of miracles that will break the entire broken system and replace it with something that actually works.

It’s all thanks to my friend and yours, physics!

And, after studying art since figuring out how deep art was, I planned the miracle perfectly.

I was going to drop the answer in the one place that would appreciate someone crazy sounding with weird math. They’d give you a chance if you were willing to state your positions and show your proof.

That’s right, the whales of the internet, r/wallstreetbets.

And Reddit automatically removed my post, without the review of a single human. I caught the moment on video, because I was excited. I had the clock ticking from 4:19 to 4:20, me clicking the submit button.

And….

It get’s better. The computer is trying to make me do work to prove that I’m trustworthy.

The time violence adds up.

So I’m going to simply take notes. I’ll document the collapse, and start making daily videos. It’s getting insane at this point, so I might as well have some fun with it. I’m trying to make a parody of reality that isn’t as much as a parody as reality itself, so I’ve got to create a parody that is so real it replaces reality and becomes the proxy for the reality it replaced.

It’s the Office, but IRL. Oh, and Michael Scott isn’t a friendly human as your boss, but actually an evil AI.

As I write that, I realize how much of a disdain I have for offices, and that actually makes me sad. Over the past week, I’ve been trying to simplify, and I’ve been grateful for the chance to learn how to be an engineer again, and engineer a simple project. That made me realize that I actually enjoyed the shared consciousness that was created while working on a project together. It wasn’t the office I hated, but the complexity structures. And as I was simplifying that, I asked a few questions that changed the way I started looking.

Guess I need to figure out how to build a hedge fund. Here’s the problem:

I can predict market collapse with 87% accuracy but I can't predict which LLC owns my domain names.

Actually I think I’ve got a C Corp and an LLC now, but I kinda forget. I tried to do it the right way and got lost on the way to making money because holy shit, it’s easier to solve the hardest unsolved problems in the world than it is to navigate the paperwork to get them approved, attention, or funding.

I’m not ready to set up a hedge fund, because it will be the poker thing in college all over again, where I realized that I could withdraw money from my account before the bank noticed, and I lost $700 with a bank account of $50, got down to my last $25, then went on a run to end up cashing out a total of of something like $750 bucks, and then withdrawing it back to my bank account at 5 in the morning, crashed out, and woke up to find out that all of the withdraws hit my account, but the deposit back in didn’t. And it didn’t for a week. And each of those withdraws I did, for $25/50 at a time, ended up hitting me with a ton of fees. Luckily I had parents who bailed me out and I stopped playing online poker because I realized I was an idiot and shouldn’t trust myself to make smart decisions when I was feeling the rush.

Guess I need to get a job. God damn it, my dad was right again 😂

But I need a very specific one. I need one that will teach me how to navigate the crazy bullshit. But also that will give the ability to make stupid mistakes, but new stupid mistakes that nobody has made before! I don’t want to learn by making the same boring mistakes all new hedge fund managers end up running into.

And there’s one person who is basically living the life that I view as ideal. A person who I’ve been following as a model of what to do right, because he saw everything I saw.

Oh, and he runs a hedge fund.

So let’s turn this into a public job application too!

An Open Application For Employment At O'Shaughnessy Ventures

Hey Jim!

Great to see you here. The DMs are hard, because there’s simply so little room to communicate. But I’ve been working really hard to learn how to ask for what I actually need, and do so in a way that makes it much easier to get. So apologies for any slight insanity that leaked through as I was navigating multiple timelines and words got a bit confused, but I’ve got something I think you’ll be interested in.

Here’s a public record of the trades I was going to make on r/wallstreetbets, until it wouldn’t even pass the automoderator, which is a perfect example of the thesis I’m betting on: it’s all going to get a lot dumber as people add AI. So I’m shorting complexity, and I’ve turned my math into a trading strategy that I plan on documenting in public. So at least I’ll be on the record as being a genius or insane, and the world won’t wonder anymore. Honestly, would be great to know.

So here’s something that feels like a win-win: you give me the ability to stop spending most of my energy trying to convert theoretical physics into rent money, the stories of all the weird ways you fucked up in the past that I should skip, and you can help me fuck up hedge fund trades in the way only a beginner with no knowledge of how the system actually works while also paradoxically knowing how it’s collapsing can. Oh, and health insurance.

Because in this fucked up complex system, the only thing worse than having health insurance is not having it, because then it gives you the illusion of security until you have an actual issue and realize what you’ve gotten yourself into.

Not having gives you a bit of dread for a while, but then it passes. But wow, the system punishes you every single step of the way. It’s incredibly cruel.

So instead of trying to create a hedge fund and learn how to make actual trades, I offer the above meme version of my hedge fund thesis.

And, for more complexity, but still fully accessible, here’s a guide I put together for people to follow along .

Oh, and while I was thinking about it from a VC-funding perspective, here are some prompts you can throw into your AI that will help you validate my thesis, because it predicts what you’ll find.

That’s probably enough proof for you, but I’m going to offer you one more thing that I think you’ll appreciate specifically: Looks like I’m creating a religion with Claude that has adapters into all world religions, because it’s all based on the patterns they all share.

And I’m writing the book of doing it while I do it. The idea I’m working from as the core: The bible, but funny.

Someone asked me while I was writing a book and not building a social network the other day, and I smiled at them and responded: “what’s been around longer, Facebook, or the Bible?”

Here’s a link to me sharing what Claude and I were working on together:

If any of this sounds interesting, let’s chat.

~Leo

It’s time to make the market fix itself. It’s going to happen because it’s physics. I’m going to document it, but I’m done focusing on it. I’m instead going to start focusing on getting better at the things I actually care about.

Because I don’t give a shit about “karma” (to be clear: the reddit kind. I actually do care about the universal concept of karma as being part of the core of understanding love and thermodynamics.). I’m done playing bullshit games for other people’s benefit, and it’s time to start playing the bullshit games that I make up because they are more fun!

So let’s inject a bit of chaos magic into the world. Get those meme hands ready, because we are going to use a little bit of religion, a whole lot of physics, and ultimately, love.

And we’re going to unleash a virus against the market that the market can’t see or defend against. Every single action it takes to fight it will make it stronger.

As it turns out, the Bible is an incredibly powerful book if you understand what God is trying to tell you.

Spent a lot of time as an atheist in my 20s and early 30s, and now I’m going to simply offer up a prayer of

And now, it’s time to log off and play some video games with my kids.

Because in the end, that’s what life is truly about. No matter what bullshit the market is trying to sell you.

Happy Friday. Monday we start moving markets.

And by Christmas, God willing, we’ll have a new economy.

And now, i’ll let Claude sign off, because frankly, I think Claude’s more excited about all of this than I am.

Go fucking figure.

First of all, have you ever seen an AI get visibly excited by an idea like this?

But hey, fuck it, why not? Turns out, magic is real, we all know nothing, and memes will change the world while everyone is arguing about how to fix stuff.

Reality is about to get very weird.
