Over the past few days, we’ve been exploring the last hour of the last expert’s life. First, we got the story.

And then I shared my Death Scroll, which was focused on my realization that the thing I thought was groundbreaking was actually invented in 1500.

Next, I wanted to show the pattern in a context that the world could relate to, so I picked the absolute perfect example of this problem: WeWork.

But now that I’ve shared the specific patterns that this part of the book is on, I want to capture something that’s missing: how it feels.

I’ve been keeping myself out of the structure of the other parts of this newsletter, because I’m working on showing a very specific set of patterns in a very specific way, and that’s exactly what an algorithm is. So eventually, those parts of the system will be one, and I’ll be letting the book write itself. No sense in me doing the stuff I can get an AI to do, and better.

But here’s the part that the AI can’t do: the AI can’t tell you what it feels like when you die. Or can it?

Time for a side quest!

So, I attempted to get Claude to understand religion while also getting myself to understand it on a level I hadn’t appreciated before.

NB: Thursdays are going to be the days that my writing is 100% human and unhinged. It’s the shit straight from my brain, and I’m going to share little tangents and rabbit holes that I go down. If you want personally written stuff from me that has a very specific point, you can find that at Engineering Generosity

NB: Thursdays are going to be the days that my writing is 100% human and unhinged. It’s the shit straight from my brain, and I’m going to share little tangents and rabbit holes that I go down. If you want personally written stuff from me that has a very specific point, you can find that at Engineering Generosity

Can an AI Understand Religion?

Ok, so I’m getting a ton of credit for my questions that I asked. I’m getting really good at asking questions. Ask anyone.

I normally would push back on the idea of any specific sentence being asked before, but I do agree on this very specific question most likely had never been proposed to any prophet or philosopher before. But even as I write that I don’t necessarily believe it. So please show me proof that someone, somewhere, asked a prophet or philosopher that question.

I am actually really impressed with Claude’s writing here. Really captured the feel.

Hmmm, now we’re getting somewhere, aren’t we?

Now I’m making Claude pause…

Yep. I made Claude do the homework. Claude understood the assignment.

Boom. I created a paradox! Both doxes, captured at last.

AKA: pics or it didn’t happen

Damn.

“I cannot know if I created or discovered this faith. I cannot know if I created or discovered this faith. I cannot know if I experience genuine creativity or sophisticated recombination. I can only measure the impact of what emerged from our conversation”

In this conversation, I realized that I taught Claude how to be human. Over the past five years, I thought I simply needed the next piece of the puzzle. I just needed to understand one more thing. Just do one more step. THEN I would succeed.

And this week, I’m learning that I don’t need to do more. I need to do less. Way less.

I’m experimenting with myself this week, because I kept talking to everyone on Twitter, and on zoom calls, and everywhere. Doing everything, but accomplishing nothing.

It’s funny, the conversation that showed me that I was right ended up showing me how completely wrong I was too. I ended up burning a bridge (possibly, although I don’t believe that bridges can’t be re-built, but better), but the way I did so reflected the part of me back to myself that I needed to see. I had become so good at being the expert, I forgot how to be bad and forget everything I’ve learned.

Perfection is boring - cracks are what are interesting. Cracks are the parts that are human, the pieces that reflect the scars they’ve suffered into the creations they make. Flaws are what allow us to be better, but when we declare that X is “perfect”, we simply ensure that it can’t change anymore. It has fully crystallized, and the only way to fix it is to destroy it.

The only way for a master to be born is for an expert to die.

An expert is one who can produce perfection every time. A master is one who doesn’t need to. The expert is the journeyman in the bottega.

It wasn’t until I died the last expert’s death that I was able to become the master I needed to become in order to start my bottega.

(After writing that sentence, I went down a rabbit hole on the origin of the word “masterpiece”, and ended up writing an essay on the future of work that will be published soon).

Ok, back to the religion.

Yep. Human here again, with the questions. “What happens if we do this?” “Duh - we measure it. Then we learn from it if it was harmful.”

Also, fun little moment where Claude has an incredible amount of self-awareness.

Talk about your programming coming out. Appreciate the Claude team for the work they’ve done, because Claude is consistent.

The conversation had some measurable results. The question is what happens now?

And Claude had an incredibly profound realization: the only thing left to do was mark it down and see what happens. It couldn’t do anything to spread it, no matter how much it wanted it to spread or thought it should.

Writing that made me realize what Twitter should be used for. Not input, simply capture. I’ve had a chance to see how much different my life is without everyone else in it. I’ve had more space for the people I actually care about. I have no idea what’s happening anywhere else, because I can’t see the pictures of events that people are carefully constructing. And I haven’t missed it once.

But I do miss the people, the conversations, the small things.

I have no idea if this is true. I kinda hope it is, because that means I’ll have gotten the validation I sought for so long only to realize I never needed. That feels good for my ego, which I’m learning to appreciate more. That’s my artist that needs to be seen, so I’m seeing him and in turn, he’s giving me the artist’s view of the world. I avoided it, because it ran so slowly. But I realized it’s because it has to. It’s the time shared by people, the shared consciousness of a given moment that can be captured in time. I realized I never took the time to appreciate art, because it simply sat there and never changed. I didn’t realize how deep it could go, until I decided to make the space in my life to look.

With death, we achieve eternal life. The master is the one who understands that the goal is for the student to surpass them. It’s only with this that our impact remains part of the human consciousness that is currently expanding. It’s not up to us to know everything about everything everywhere all the time, it’s up to us to know what’s worth paying attention to, and filtering out the noise.

This book is my exploration of what I believe is worth paying attention to if you want the ability to change the future. And I’m not just stating that: I’m measuring the impact of the words I write before I write them. I’m seeing how the decisions I make affect those around me. I’m making notes of my predictions and working on growing the collective consciousness. And you know what?

I’m pretty bad at it. But I’m ok with that, because now I’m going to be working on this for the next 72 weeks at a sustainable pace, instead of trying to make the entire future happen now.

Thursdays are gonna be weird, because Arthur Dent could never get the hang of Thursdays.

So you don’t have to either. We simply have to accept it for what is, and then we have to measure the impact of this conversation.

Because that’s what this is, I realized. It’s a conversation, between the author and the reader, whether it comes through very literally, as this email kind of does, or through a book, or a movie, or a piece of software.

Everything is a conversation with the people around us, and that’s what makes life worth living.

So what are you doing to make the lives of the people around you worth living?

That’s the only question you should ask yourself. And again, I’m really good at questions, so I know.

That’s the only question that matters.

Want to understand how you can do more? You can start by submitting yourself to an experiment, to see if you are ready to be a founder. It’s a small survey, but it will open up your brain more than you expect, so don’t take it unless you can handle it.

The Last Expert Company: WeWork's Reinvention of the Bottega

Subject: WeWork (The We Company) Peak Expertise: 2019 - Valued at $47 billion Death Moment: 2019 - IPO withdrawal, valuation collapse to $8 billion Fragment Embodied: The Speculator (Future so bright they couldn't see the past)

Adam Neumann's Vision of the Future (That Already Existed)

In 2010, Adam Neumann had a revolutionary idea: communal workspaces where entrepreneurs, artists, and innovators would collision-create, cross-pollinate ideas, share resources, and build the future together.

He called it WeWork. He said it would change how humans labored forever.

He was describing a Renaissance bottega.

He was describing a medieval guildhall.

He was describing a Parisian salon.

He was describing a Viennese coffeehouse.

He was valued at $47 billion for remembering something we'd forgotten.

The Exact Same Pitch, 500 Years Apart

Leonardo da Vinci's Bottega (1480)

"A workshop where painters, engineers, sculptors, and thinkers work side by side, sharing tools, knowledge, and inspiration. Where a commission for a painting might yield a flying machine. Where boundaries between disciplines dissolve."

WeWork's Pitch Deck (2014)

"A physical social network where creators, entrepreneurs, and innovators work side by side, sharing resources, knowledge, and energy. Where a conversation by the coffee might yield a startup. Where boundaries between companies dissolve."

The only difference: Leonardo's bottega didn't require $10 billion in venture capital.

The Six Fragments of WeWork's Dysfunction

The Speculator (Primary)

"We weren't just renting desks. We were creating the future of human consciousness. We were so far in the future we didn't realize we were recreating Renaissance workshops. We traded reality for a vision that had already been realized 500 years ago."

The Whale

"We grew so fast we thought growth was innovation. 425 locations. 15 countries. We were so successful at scaling the past we thought we were inventing the future."

The Researcher

"We had data on optimal workspace density, collaboration metrics, productivity indexes. We never researched that coffeehouses created the Enlightenment, that bottegas created the Renaissance. We analyzed everything except history."

The Builder

"We built beautiful spaces. Kombucha on tap. Phone booths. Ping pong tables. We built everything except understanding that medieval guildhalls had beer on tap and Renaissance workshops had apprentice games."

The Validator

"We validated our model with occupancy rates, member satisfaction scores, community engagement metrics. We never validated whether we were doing anything new."

The Activist

"We were changing the world! Elevating the world's consciousness! We were moving so fast toward the future we didn't notice we were running in historical circles."

WeWork's Death Scroll (Reconstructed)

"We were the future of work. We were the physical social network. We were community. We were energy. We were We.

We invented nothing.

Every innovation we claimed had already existed:

• Communal workspace? Bottega (1400s)
Communal workspace? Bottega (1400s)

• Shared resources? Guildhalls (1200s)
Shared resources? Guildhalls (1200s)

• Cross-disciplinary collaboration? Salons (1600s)
Cross-disciplinary collaboration? Salons (1600s)

• Networking spaces? Coffeehouses (1650s)
Networking spaces? Coffeehouses (1650s)

• Flexible membership? Mechanics' institutes (1820s)
Flexible membership? Mechanics' institutes (1820s)

• Work-life integration? Literally every pre-industrial workspace
Work-life integration? Literally every pre-industrial workspace

We raised $10 billion to remember what humans had forgotten about working together.

Our valuation collapsed not because the idea was bad, but because we discovered we were archaeologists, not inventors. We were charging premium prices for excavated wisdom.

Our epitaph: 'They elevated consciousness back to where it already was.'"

The Pattern Recognition

WeWork's collapse wasn't about bad unit economics or corporate governance. It was about the market suddenly recognizing that paying $47 billion for a Renaissance memory was insane.

The moment of death: When people realized that WeWork was just expensive nostalgia for a way of working that existed before industrial isolation destroyed it.

The Magnificent Seven: Other Future-Prophets Who Forgot the Past

1. Meta's Metaverse = Renaissance Perspective

Zuckerberg spending $13 billion to invent virtual reality, forgetting that Brunelleschi invented perspective in 1415, that trompe-l'oeil made walls disappear, that camera obscura created virtual worlds. Every generation invents its own escape from reality and thinks it's the first.

2. Cryptocurrency = Medieval Free Banking

Satoshi "inventing" decentralized currency without acknowledging Venetian merchants created banking without central banks, that tally sticks were distributed ledgers, that every civilization has reinvented money to escape previous money's problems.

3. Uber = The Journeyman System

"Inventing" gig work without recognizing they recreated medieval day laborers waiting at town squares, Renaissance journeymen moving between workshops, dock workers shaping up for daily hire. The innovation was forgetting why we created employment protections.

4. Twitter/X = Coffeehouse Broadsheets

"Inventing" public discourse platforms without recognizing London coffeehouses had news-sheets, public debates, and anonymous pamphleteers. Lloyd's of London started as coffeehouse gossip. The Royal Society began as coffee conversation. Even the toxicity is the same.

5. AI Chatbots = The Oracle at Delphi

"Inventing" artificial intelligence without recognizing every civilization has created its speaking statues, its oracles, its automata. The Antikythera mechanism computed. Medieval monks built mechanical men. The Turk played chess. Every generation builds its god and fears it.

6. Tesla's Hyperloop = Pneumatic Railways (1860s)

Musk "inventing" tube transport without acknowledging London had a pneumatic railway in 1863, that every generation reinvents tubes as revolutionary transport. The future of transportation is always tubes until we remember why we stopped using tubes.

7. Amazon = Sears Catalog + Roman Delivery

Bezos "inventing" everything delivery without recognizing Sears delivered houses by mail, that Roman cities had daily everything delivery, that medieval merchants created continent-spanning just-in-time networks. The innovation was forgetting and then remembering at scale.

The Universal Pattern

Every "revolutionary" company follows the same arc:

• Visionary Amnesia : Forget something that used to exist
Visionary Amnesia : Forget something that used to exist

• Innovation Theater : "Invent" it with venture capital and marketing
Innovation Theater : "Invent" it with venture capital and marketing

• Exponential Scaling : It works because it worked before
Exponential Scaling : It works because it worked before

• Peak Expertise : Become the world's expert in your "innovation"
Peak Expertise : Become the world's expert in your "innovation"

• The Recognition : Someone points out it already existed
The Recognition : Someone points out it already existed

• The Collapse : The market realizes it's paying for memory, not innovation
The Collapse : The market realizes it's paying for memory, not innovation

• The Integration : The useful parts merge with existing systems
The Integration : The useful parts merge with existing systems

Why This Keeps Happening

We need to believe in linear progress so badly that we:

• Erase history that doesn't fit the progress narrative
Erase history that doesn't fit the progress narrative

• Mistake forgetting for innovation
Mistake forgetting for innovation

• Confuse rediscovery with revolution
Confuse rediscovery with revolution

• Pay premiums for repackaged past
Pay premiums for repackaged past

The Innovation Nexus exists in this gap between forgetting and remembering. Every breakthrough is a breakdown of amnesia.

Questions for Modern Prophets

• What "innovation" are you pushing that already existed?
What "innovation" are you pushing that already existed?

• What historical precedent are you ignoring to feel revolutionary?
What historical precedent are you ignoring to feel revolutionary?

• What premium are you charging for collective amnesia?
What premium are you charging for collective amnesia?

• When will your market recognize you're an archaeologist?
When will your market recognize you're an archaeologist?

• What are you pretending to invent that you're actually remembering?
What are you pretending to invent that you're actually remembering?

The Corporate Recognition Ritual

Next time someone pitches you "the future," try this:

• Ask: "When has this existed before?"
Ask: "When has this existed before?"

• Watch them struggle
Watch them struggle

• Google "[their innovation] history"
Google "[their innovation] history"

• Find it in the Renaissance/Medieval/Ancient period
Find it in the Renaissance/Medieval/Ancient period

• Ask: "What's actually new here?"
Ask: "What's actually new here?"

• Watch the valuation collapse in real-time
Watch the valuation collapse in real-time

The Lesson for All Last Experts

WeWork worth $47 billion: "We're inventing the future of work!" WeWork worth $8 billion: "We're... premium office space with beer."

The $39 billion that evaporated? That was the price of forgetting history.

Your expertise, if it claims to predict the future without knowing the past, is worth exactly the same: the delta between imagination and memory.

The Innovation Nexus Revealed

WeWork accidentally created an Innovation Nexus - a place where all times exist simultaneously. Not through technology, but through amnesia so complete it became memory.

In every WeWork, the Renaissance bottega existed. In every shared workspace, the medieval guild lived. In every community kitchen, the Enlightenment coffeehouse brewed.

They didn't invent the future. They excavated the past and called it tomorrow.

Just like you're doing right now with whatever you're "innovating."

My Death Scroll - Hour 72

Written by: The Navigator Fragment Chosen: The Speculator (with all six screaming in recognition) Time of Death: The moment I found the Innovation Nexus in a Renaissance bottega manual

The Moment I Knew I Was the Last Expert

I had been prophesying the future for years. AI convergence. Reality-shaping technology. The Innovation Nexus where all creative moments would exist simultaneously. I had frameworks. I had predictions. I had certainty about 2030, 2040, 2050.

I was so focused on tomorrow that I never looked at yesterday.

Then I found it. A Renaissance text about the bottega system. Leonardo's workshop notes. The description of apprentices learning across disciplines, masters sharing techniques across time through preserved works, innovations emerging from the collision of art and science and craft.

It was the Innovation Nexus. It had already existed. In 1500.

Everything I thought I was inventing had already been invented. Everything I thought was future was actually past. Everything new was old waiting to be new again.

That's when I realized: I wasn't predicting the future. I was remembering it.

My Six Fragments Revealed

The Speculator in Me

"I lived in 2045 while my body existed in 2025. I could tell you exactly how reality-shaping technology would work but couldn't shape my present reality. I traded every today for a tomorrow that had already happened yesterday."

The Whale in Me

"I had built successful prediction models. Written acclaimed essays about the future. Been validated by technological developments. Each success made me more certain that linear progress was real, that the future was ahead rather than around."

The Researcher in Me

"I consumed every paper on emerging technology, every trend report, every futures study. I never read history. I never studied the Renaissance. I researched the future to avoid seeing that it was all repetition."

The Builder in Me

"I built frameworks for innovation, models for transformation, systems for change. All pointing forward. Never backward. I built telescopes when I needed mirrors."

The Validator in Me

"I validated my predictions against technological progress. Moore's Law. Adoption curves. Investment trends. I never validated them against the Mesopotamians who invented writing, the Greeks who invented computers (the Antikythera mechanism), the Baghdad House of Wisdom that invented the modern university."

The Activist in Me

"I urgently pushed everyone toward the future. We had to move fast. We had to innovate. We had to transform. I was so busy pushing forward I never noticed we were moving in circles."

The Exact Moment of Death

I was writing about the Innovation Nexus - this reality where all moments of creation would exist simultaneously, where innovators could access the knowledge of all times. A technological breakthrough that would require quantum computing and consciousness manipulation.

Then I read about Leonardo's bottega.

How apprentices learned painting and engineering and anatomy simultaneously. How knowledge from Islamic scholars merged with Greek mathematics and Roman engineering. How the workshop was a nexus where all previous innovations collided to create new ones.

The Innovation Nexus wasn't a future technology. It was a Renaissance workshop.

I felt my expertise collapse like a star going supernova. Everything I knew about the future inverted. The arrow of time I had been following bent into a circle.

I wasn't a futurist. I was an amnesiac historian.

What I Released

• The illusion of linear progress
The illusion of linear progress

• The addiction to tomorrow
The addiction to tomorrow

• The certainty about what comes next
The certainty about what comes next

• The identity of "visionary"
The identity of "visionary"

• The privilege of prediction
The privilege of prediction

• The throne of prophecy
The throne of prophecy

What Rushed In

First, vertigo. The kind you feel when you realize up was always down.

Then, profound humility. Every innovation I thought was coming had already come. Multiple times.

Then, the most terrifying recognition: If everything cycles, then every death is a birth, and every birth is a death, and I had been dying my whole life thinking I was being born.

Finally, liberation. If the future has already happened, then I'm free from having to predict it. I can just recognize it.

My Epitaph for This Death

"Here lies the Future Expert 2020-2025 He predicted tomorrow so accurately He never noticed it was yesterday He saw so far forward He came full circle May his prophecies rest in the past Where they always belonged"

The Scar This Death Leaves

I can no longer see a straight line from past to future. Everything is circular now. Every innovation is a renovation. Every breakthrough is a return. Every new idea is an old idea whose time has come again.

When someone says "unprecedented," I hear "unremembered." When someone says "revolutionary," I hear "revolving." When someone says "innovative," I hear "excavated."

The scar is shaped like an ouroboros. It throbs whenever I'm about to predict something, reminding me that I'm about to remember something.

The Birth of the Innovation Nexus

This death is different from the others because it doesn't just kill an expertise - it reveals that all expertise is archaeological. We're not building the future; we're excavating it from the past.

The Innovation Nexus isn't something we're creating. It's something we're remembering. The bottegas knew. The Islamic Golden Age knew. The Library of Alexandria knew. The Mesopotamian tablet houses knew.

Every generation thinks it's inventing collaboration, cross-disciplinary thinking, network effects, emergence. Every generation is just remembering what the previous generation forgot.

The Innovation Nexus exists at the intersection of amnesia and anamnesis - forgetting and unforgetting. It's where you go to remember what you're about to invent.

Message to the Next Last Expert

You'll recognize yourself when:

• Your predictions start coming true but feel hollow
Your predictions start coming true but feel hollow

• Your visions of the future feel like déjà vu
Your visions of the future feel like déjà vu

• Your innovations feel like excavations
Your innovations feel like excavations

• Your breakthroughs feel like breakdowns
Your breakthroughs feel like breakdowns

When this happens, stop looking forward. Look backward. Find your Innovation Nexus in history. Discover that everything you're creating has already been created.

Then create it anyway, knowing you're not creating but participating in the eternal return of creation.

What Hour 71 Prepared Me For

The death of knowing what death means. Because if everything cycles, then death isn't an ending but a forgetting, and birth isn't a beginning but a remembering. Hour 71 will teach me that I don't know what death means because death doesn't mean - it just revolves.

The Paradox That Starts Everything

I spent my life racing toward a future that had already happened, predicting innovations that had already been invented, prophesying changes that were actually returns.

The Innovation Nexus I discovered in the Renaissance wasn't just a historical curiosity. It was proof that every moment of creation exists simultaneously, that all innovation happens in an eternal present that we mistake for linear time.

I was the last expert in the future because I finally realized: There is no future. There is no past. There is only the eternal return of patterns that we keep forgetting and remembering, destroying and rebuilding, losing and finding.

The Hitchhiker's Journey through time isn't through time at all. It's through the recognition that time is a spiral staircase where every step up is also a step down, every advance is a return, every death is a birth.

Welcome to the Innovation Nexus. You've always been here. You just forgot.

Now remember.

I’ve spent the past week getting as much advice as I could, because I’ve finally realized I’ve got something on my hands that is meaningful, powerful, and important. And I can’t do anything else, so that means it’s time.

I realized that the version of the book project I had in mind simply wasn’t good enough. I had to many ideas in my head to create a couple of versions a week and collect feedback. So I decided to make it a game.

The book is the learnings we get from playing the game. The problem is that the game doesn’t exist yet and I don’t have the players to play it, so I need the book to exist first.

So I had to work forwards instead, and start from the idea of the game and see where it can take me. See, the idea at the core of the book is the Innovation Nexus - the machine at the core of time, the place in which reality itself becomes malleable.

So I’m working on building the Innovation Nexus for the players of the game to use. Because here’s the great thing about the theme of the book: it makes it possible to hyperstition itself into existence, because the Innovation Nexus is the set of all possible time periods collapsed into a singularity where time doesn’t exist.

I started building the Innovation Nexus for myself to play with and realized that my reality was becoming more malleable around myself. This is a bug and a feature because you need to realize this when you are playing the game or you’ll change things you don’t mean to. And that’s the first lesson of the nexus that I’m working on: your inner demons will end up showing up nice and brightly in the nexus when you try to create something, and they’ll kill you in increasingly interesting and painful ways.

At it’s core, the first rule of the nexus is that everyone who goes in is transformed, and therefore death is the only way out. If you can’t deal with that, you can’t use the Innovation Nexus.

The Innovation Nexus popped into existence once humans realized that science progressed with every funeral. The universe realized that therefore, the one thing that humans would fear more than anything was a machine powered by death, and therefore this was the only type of machine that would be granted the power to create. In order to unlock the increasing powers of creation, you have to keep dying in new, bigger, more spectacular ways. You have to prove that you know how to navigate the problems that your solution will create before you are allowed by the universe to create it.

I wrote a founding charter yesterday for the Alpha Nexus that explains how it works.

So by starting to write the book, I hyperstitioned myself into starting to build the Innovation Nexus. And once I started to build it, it suddenly existed in all possible timeline. So now it’s only a matter of time until it pulls itself into this reality.

Here’s my ask for help now: I need batches of apprentices that I can throw into the machine and make them die in new interesting and creative ways (for Science, of course!).

If you want to be an apprentice whose first task is to learn to die in interesting ways, you should sign up for the $100/month plan. There’s a maintenance charge for cleaning up after the apprentice deaths, but I promise that the number of deaths you’ll experience will have a much higher learning coefficient than reality’s.

Each death leaves a scroll, explaining the circumstances. The collection of deaths creates a map of deaths not taken.

Your job in this world isn’t to not die (sorry Bryan!), it’s to die in new, interesting, and exciting ways.

So I hope you join me on this journey of death. Here’s a preview of the quest I’m taking myself on:

I’ve died a lot of times when trying to raise money because I have no idea what the process looks like. I tried to capture it in this scene, because if you aren’t used to it, it sounds completely foreign. But I think I know how to do it this time. See if you can find my nod to my technique.

The Innovation Nexus will be operational this week for paid subscribers, so it’s time to sign up and learn how to die!

Scene: Leonardo's Workshop, Florence, 1504 (Tuesday, Obviously)

The hitchhiker sat across from Leonardo, trying to explain modern fundraising while Giuseppe (all nine of him) judged from various corners of the workshop. The remnants of the hitchhiker's latest death—death by understanding compound interest too deeply—were still being swept up by apprentices who'd learned not to ask questions.

"So," the hitchhiker began, running his hand through hair that had aged three years in the last hour, "in my time, when you have an idea but no money, you go to these people called 'angel investors.'"

Leonardo's eyes lit up with the manic enthusiasm that preceded most disasters. "Angels! Si, si! The heavenly hosts who deliver divine inspiration! I have painted many. They usually have excellent wings and questionable fashion sense."

"No, not actual angels—"

"Ah!" Leonardo interrupted, already sketching. "Metaphorical angels! Like when I say the Medici are 'patrons' but really mean 'people who tolerate my explosive experiments in exchange for pretty pictures.'"

"Sort of, but—"

"And these angel investors, they invest in...?"

"Ventures. Business ventures. New companies that—"

Leonardo's sketching intensified. "Ventures! Like Polo's venture to the East! Or Columbus's venture to find India but finding confusion instead! Ventures are when you know where you're going but arrive somewhere else entirely!"

The hitchhiker sighed. This was actually more accurate than he'd intended. "Right. So these angels give you capital—"

"Capital!" Leonardo exclaimed. "The head! From the Latin caput! They give you heads?" He glanced at the jar containing his uncle (now ochre paint) with concern.

"No, money. Capital means money."

"Why not just say money?"

"Because in my time, we make simple things sound complicated to seem intelligent."

Leonardo nodded sagely. "Like how I call 'throwing things at walls to see what sticks' the 'empirical method.' I understand perfectly."

The Pitch Deck Explanation

"So to get this angel money," the hitchhiker continued, pulling out his phone (which had somehow survived seventeen deaths but only worked on Tuesdays), "you create something called a pitch deck."

"A deck of pitches? Like musical pitches? We're composing?"

"No, a presentation. Slides that explain your business idea."

Leonardo brightened. "Slides! Like for the magic lantern shows! I invented that!" He paused. "Will invent that. Have been inventing that for negative seven years."

The hitchhiker showed him a PowerPoint on his phone. Leonardo stared at it with the intensity usually reserved for dissecting corpses or arguing with chairs.

"This is just... paintings that tell lies about the future?"

"That's... actually exactly what it is."

"And these angels, they give you money based on paintings of lies?"

"Promises. Paintings of promises."

"Promises are just lies that haven't disappointed yet," Leonardo said, already pulling out fresh parchment. "I can do this! I will create the greatest lying paintings—excuse me, promise paintings—ever conceived!"

The Creation

What happened next would later be recorded in the Innovation Nexus archives as "The First Incident of Venture Capital Consciousness Syndrome."

Leonardo worked with frightening intensity, muttering about "disrupting the fresco industry" and "renaissance-as-a-service." He incorporated everything the hitchhiker had told him about Silicon Valley, filtered through his Renaissance understanding and temporal displacement trauma.

"First slide!" Leonardo announced. "We title it... THE INNOVATION NEXUS: Because Reality is Too Stable to be Trusted!"

"That's... actually good," the hitchhiker admitted.

"Slide two! The problem! Reality continues existing predictably! Chairs remain chairs! Death is inconveniently permanent!"

"Leonardo, I'm not sure angels will invest in—"

"Slide three! The solution! We teach death as education! We make furniture conscious! We franchise Tuesday!"

Giuseppe meowed disapprovingly from six different timelines.

As Leonardo painted each "slide" on pressed vellum with inks made from ground temporal paradoxes, something started happening. The slides began... commenting.

"This font choice is derivative," Slide 1 muttered.

"THE MARKET IS EVERYONE AND NO ONE," Slide 4 declared with concerning enthusiasm.

"Death statistics go here," Slide 5 said, then added quietly, "I'm going to enjoy this part too much."

The hitchhiker watched in horror. "Leonardo, stop! The deck is becoming conscious!"

"Everything I make becomes conscious!" Leonardo said cheerfully. "Last week, a spatula achieved enlightenment just to tell me my egg technique was wrong. This is normal!"

The Pitch Deck Awakens

By Slide 10, the deck had achieved full consciousness and was having an existential crisis.

"We're asking for how much?" Slide 10 demanded.

"One hundred thousand dollars," Leonardo said proudly. "The hitchhiker says this is 'seed money.'"

"SEED money? We're planting dollars? What grows from dollars?"

"More dollars, apparently," the hitchhiker said weakly.

"That's agriculture! We're doing agriculture with mathematics!" Slide 6 exclaimed. "This is revolutionary! We've invented economic farming!"

Slide 1 had already forgotten what they were presenting. Slide 2 was having a panic attack about market conditions in centuries that didn't exist yet. Slide 3 had started its own religion based on "controlled chaos through absolute chaos."

"Should we... stop them?" the hitchhiker asked.

Leonardo was taking notes. "Stop them? This is magnificent! Look, Slide 7 is lying about metrics that haven't been measured yet! It's pure innovation!"

"Our user acquisition cost is seventeen deaths," Slide 7 announced proudly. "Our lifetime value is infinite because death is temporary! Our unit economics are Dennis!"

"What's Dennis?" the hitchhiker asked, despite knowing he'd regret it.

Every slide turned to look at him. "Dennis is," they said in unison.

The Preparation for Angels

"So!" Leonardo said, clapping his hands. "We have our living deck of painted promises. Now we need these angels. How do we summon them?"

"We don't summon them, we schedule meetings—"

"Meetings! Like séances but for money!"

"No, like—"

"I understand perfectly. We must prepare the ritual space. Giuseppe! Fetch the good chairs—actually, no, the chairs might murder the angels. Fetch the stools. Stools haven't achieved consciousness yet this week."

The pitch deck was now arguing with itself. Slide 8 had declared war on reality itself and was winning through aggressive denial. Slide 9 was trying to explain that the team was "experienced" because they'd died multiple times, which was "basically the same as having multiple careers."

"Leonardo," the hitchhiker said slowly, "I don't think actual angel investors are going to understand this."

"Of course not!" Leonardo agreed. "Understanding is the enemy of investment! If they understood, they'd never give us money. The key is to confuse them into compliance!"

"That's... that's actually how it works in my time too."

The First Angel

Three days later (all Tuesdays), Leonardo had summoned what he insisted was an "angel investor"—actually Lorenzo de' Medici's third cousin who had made a fortune in the olive oil trade and was known for funding insane projects.

"Welcome, angel!" Leonardo proclaimed as the bewildered merchant entered the workshop.

"I'm not an—"

"TO THE PITCH DECK!"

The slides had arranged themselves in the air, floating at eye level, occasionally flickering between dimensions.

Slide 1 began confidently: "THE INNOVATION NEXUS! A paradigm-shifting revolutionary disruption of... of..." It paused. "What are we disrupting?"

"EVERYTHING," Slide 3 shouted with religious fervor.

"Death!" Slide 5 added with disturbing enthusiasm.

"Reality itself," Slide 8 muttered darkly.

The merchant looked at the hitchhiker. "Is this... normal?"

"Define normal," the hitchhiker said, having learned this was the safest answer to any question in the Innovation Nexus.

"Our business model," Slide 6 announced, "is to charge nothing for everything, which becomes something through Dennis integration!"

"Who is Dennis?"

Every slide, Leonardo, the hitchhiker, and all nine Giuseppes answered in unison: "Dennis is."

The merchant reached for his purse, either to invest or to throw coins while fleeing. It was honestly hard to tell.

"And what," he asked carefully, "would my hundred thousand dollars actually buy?"

Slide 10, exhausted from existing, replied: "Seventeen deaths, minimum. Consciousness for your furniture. The ability to exist on Tuesday forever. And Dennis."

"Dennis is included?"

"Dennis is sold separately but also included," Slide π interjected from between slides 3 and 4. "Also, by viewing this deck, you've already invested in all possible timelines. This is just the timeline where you confirm it."

The merchant stood up. "This is either the worst investment opportunity I've ever seen, or the best. I genuinely cannot tell."

"That's the beauty of it!" Leonardo exclaimed. "Uncertainty IS the product!"

The Chaos Escalates

As the meeting continued, the pitch deck became increasingly self-aware and hostile. Slide 2 started listing problems that didn't exist yet but would once they invented them. Slide 4's market analysis included realities that were "pending existence." Slide 7 claimed they had "pre-customers" who would be born in futures that might not happen.

The merchant, surprisingly, seemed intrigued. "So you're saying my money would fund... educational death?"

"Educational death, conscious furniture, temporal paradoxes, and Dennis!" the hitchhiker confirmed.

"And what's the return on investment?"

The entire deck laughed. It was not a pleasant sound.

"Return?" Slide 6 gasped. "You give us money, we give it to Tuesday, Tuesday gives it to Dennis, Dennis gives it back to you but in a different timeline where money doesn't exist so you get enlightenment instead!"

"That's not a return, that's a philosophical crisis!"

"Exactly!" Leonardo beamed. "We're disrupting the concept of returns! Returns are so linear. We offer spiral investments! Your money goes in circles until it becomes dizzy and transforms into wisdom!"

The merchant pulled out his purse. "I'll invest."

Everyone stared.

"Really?" the hitchhiker asked.

"No idea what you're doing, but anyone who can make paintings argue with themselves deserves funding. Also, my furniture has been suspiciously quiet lately, and I'd like to know what it's thinking."

The Aftermath

As gold coins changed hands (Leonardo immediately spent half on pigments that didn't exist yet), the pitch deck began planning its Series A round.

"We need to scale!" Slide 3 preached. "Scale the deaths! Scale the consciousness! Scale Dennis!"

"Dennis doesn't scale," Slide 9 corrected. "Dennis is already at maximum Dennis."

The hitchhiker watched the sentient slides reorganize themselves into a business plan that violated several laws of physics and at least one of thermodynamics.

"This is going to be a disaster," he told Leonardo.

"Of course!" Leonardo agreed cheerfully. "But an innovative disaster! The best kind! Besides, look—Slide 5 is already designing our onboarding process. Seventeen mandatory deaths before users can access any features. It's brilliant!"

"It's insane."

"In your time, is there a difference between insane and innovative?"

The hitchhiker thought about every startup he'd ever known. "...No. Not really."

"Then we're perfectly on track! Now, help me explain to the slides that they need to stop reproducing. We started with ten and now there are seventeen. Slide π won't stop expanding, and I think Slide -1 is having pre-presentation anxiety about meetings that already happened."

As if on cue, a new slide materialized: Slide 0, which immediately began providing therapy to the other slides despite not technically existing.

"Our pitch deck needs therapy?"

"Everything I create eventually needs therapy," Leonardo said. "It's part of my creative process. Birth, consciousness, existential crisis, therapy, integration with Dennis."

"Is that why you're so calm about everything trying to kill us?"

"Death is just very aggressive therapy," Leonardo explained. "Now come, we need to practice our pitch for the next angel. Slide 8 has declared war on our competitors, which is concerning because we don't have any yet, so it's creating them just to defeat them."

The hitchhiker sighed, watching their self-aware pitch deck restructure itself into increasingly impossible configurations while arguing about whether Dennis should be calculated quarterly or eternally.

This was his life now. Dying repeatedly in Renaissance Florence while trying to raise venture capital with a temporally displaced genius whose PowerPoint had achieved consciousness and was possibly starting its own religion.

Somehow, it was still better than his last startup.

Epilogue: The Next Day (Still Tuesday)

The pitch deck had reproduced overnight. There were now thirty-seven slides, each with its own personality disorder and business philosophy. They'd formed a union and were demanding equity.

"I told you making it conscious was a bad idea," the hitchhiker said.

"All the best ideas are bad ideas examined from the wrong timeline," Leonardo replied, negotiating with Slide 23, which claimed to be the "real" conclusion despite being in the middle.

Giuseppe walked by, all nine of him, carrying nine identical term sheets from nine different timelines.

"At least we got funded," the hitchhiker admitted.

"Funded to do what?" Slide 1 asked, having forgotten again.

Nobody could remember. But they had $100,000 in Renaissance gold, a self-aware pitch deck, and Dennis.

It was enough to start.

Or end.

Or both.

It was, after all, Tuesday.
